intro.html: How often does it happen? These ten words answer that question in different ways. Some mean now and then, at no set time (sporadic, intermittent). Some mean again and again (recurrent, continual, habitual), and one means on a regular schedule (periodic). The rest mean without stopping (continuous, incessant, unremitting, persistent).
The famous pair: continual means again and again, with breaks (a dripping faucet); continuous means going on without a break (a flowing river).

words.def: happening now and then, at irregular times
words.ex: We heard only {sporadic} birdsong in the cold woods: a chirp here, then nothing for an hour.
words.ctx: The town’s internet service was {sporadic}: it might work all morning, vanish for an hour, return for ten minutes and then fail again.
words.etym: From Greek sporadikos, “scattered,” related to spora, “a sowing,” the source of spore.

mn.cue: SPORE-adic: popping up here and there
mn.text: After the rain, mushrooms pop up from scattered spores: one here, two there, none over there. They appear at {sporadic} spots and times.

scene.alt: A boy points at mushrooms that have popped up here and there in the forest.

words.def: stopping and starting again, at irregular times
words.ex: The forecast called for {intermittent} showers, stopping and starting all afternoon.
words.ctx: The signal from the stranded ship was {intermittent}; it would crackle for a few seconds, go silent for minutes, then crackle again.
words.etym: From Latin intermittere, “to leave off for a while”: inter (between) + mittere (to let go).

mn.text: The rain stops, starts and stops again, so Lila opens and shuts her umbrella all afternoon. The rain is {intermittent}.

scene.alt: A girl with an umbrella looks puzzled as a rain cloud and the sun take turns in the sky.

words.def: never stopping, often to the point of annoyance
words.ex: The puppy’s {incessant} barking went on all night without a single pause.
words.ctx: After three days of {incessant} rain, without even an hour of sunshine, the creek rose over the road.
words.etym: From Latin incessans, “unceasing”: in- (not) + cessare (to stop).

mn.text: The ants march across the picnic blanket all day long, never stopping for a moment. Their marching is {incessant}.

scene.alt: A line of ants marches nonstop toward a pie while a girl stands with her hands on her hips.

words.def: done regularly, out of long practice; usual
words.ex: Grandpa’s {habitual} morning walk, the same route every day for forty years, always ends at the bakery.
words.ctx: Being late was not a one-time slip for Max but a {habitual} problem; he missed the first bell nearly every day of the term.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin habitualis, from Latin habitus, “condition, habit.”

mn.text: Every morning at seven, Grandpa Gus walks the dog, reads the paper and drinks one cup of tea, always in that order. It is his {habitual} routine.

scene.alt: A grandfather reads his morning paper beside a cup of tea and a sleeping dog, as he does every day.

words.ex: The car needs {periodic} oil changes, one every five thousand miles, like clockwork.
words.ctx: The comet makes {periodic} visits to our skies, returning roughly every seventy-six years, so most people see it only once in a lifetime.
words.etym: From Greek periodos, “a going around, a cycle”: peri (around) + hodos (way).

mn.cue: PERIOD-ic: like the bell every PERIOD
mn.text: The school bell rings at the end of every class period, right on schedule. Its ringing is {periodic}.

scene.alt: The school bell rings on schedule as students head to their next class.

words.ex: Lost keys are a {recurrent} problem in our house; they go missing again every few weeks.
words.ctx: Flooding is a {recurrent} danger in the valley; it has returned every few springs for as long as anyone can remember.
words.etym: From Latin recurrere, “to run back, return”: re (back) + currere (to run).

mn.cue: RE-CURRENT: the current brings it back
mn.text: Kai tosses the beach ball out, and the waves carry it back to him, again and again and again. Its return is {recurrent}.

scene.alt: A wave carries a beach ball back to a laughing boy again and again.

words.def: happening again and again, with short breaks between
words.ex: The {continual} ringing of the phone, a new call every few minutes, made it hard to finish the report.
words.ctx: His {continual} interruptions, a new question every few minutes, kept the class from finishing the story.
words.etym: From Latin continuus, “hanging together, unbroken,” from continere (to hold together), the same source as continuous.
words.note: Continual: again and again, with breaks (a dripping faucet). Continuous: without any break (a flowing river).

mn.cue: continu-AL: AL asks again, and again
mn.text: Al raises his hand, asks a question, waits a minute and asks another, all day long. His questions are {continual}: again and again, with short breaks.

scene.alt: A boy named Al raises his hand with yet another question while his teacher covers his eyes.

words.ex: At rush hour the highway is one {continuous} line of cars, bumper to bumper with no gaps.
words.ctx: Unlike the old clock, which ticked forward in little jumps, the new clock’s second hand moved in one {continuous} sweep, never pausing.
words.etym: From Latin continuus, “hanging together, unbroken,” from continere (to hold together).

mn.text: The river flows past Sven’s fishing spot day and night without stopping for even a second: One Unbroken Stream. Its flow is {continuous}.

scene.alt: A fisherman sits by a river that flows on and on without a break.

words.def: refusing to give up; continuing for a long time
words.ex: The {persistent} puppy scratched at the door again and again until someone finally let him in.
words.ctx: The inventor’s first forty designs failed, but she was {persistent}, and the forty-first worked so well that she sold thousands.
words.etym: From Latin persistere, “to continue steadfastly”: per (thoroughly) + sistere (to stand).

mn.cue: PER-SISTER-ent: little sister never gives up
mn.text: Ivy asks her big brother to play catch ten times, twenty times, fifty times, until he finally says yes. Ivy is {persistent}.

scene.alt: A little girl holding a ball keeps begging her teenage brother to play.

words.ex: The hikers trudged on through the {unremitting} wind, which never eased for a moment.
words.ctx: Her success came from years of {unremitting} practice: four hours at the piano every day, through holidays and summers alike.
words.etym: From un- (not) + remit, “to slacken, ease off,” from Latin remittere, “to send back, let go.”

mn.text: Hour after hour, the desert sun blazes down on the travelers, with no cloud and no shade. The heat is {unremitting}.

scene.alt: A traveler and a camel trudge through the desert under a blazing sun.

after.cap: Sort the words by their pattern in time.

after.html: A dripping faucet is continual (drip, pause, drip). A flowing river is continuous (no pause at all). Memory trick: continu-ous = One Unbroken Stream.

items.q: The river’s flow past the mill never stops for a moment. Its flow is…
items.why: Continuous means without any break. Continual means again and again, with breaks.

items.q: The faucet dripped all night: drip, pause, drip, pause. The dripping was…
items.why: Drip, pause, drip: again and again with breaks is continual. Continuous, unremitting and incessant all mean without a break.

items.q: Which word describes something that happens on a regular schedule?
items.why: Periodic means at regular intervals (like a bell every period). Sporadic and intermittent are irregular; incessant never stops.

items.q: True or false: sporadic applause comes in scattered bursts, now and then.
items.why: True. Sporadic means happening now and then, at irregular times.
